SciVer — Multimodal Scientific Claim Verification

Each item pairs a natural-language claim with the figure/table evidence from a paper it refers to, and a gold label: Entailed or Refuted.

The benchmark's trick: Refuted claims are made by minimally perturbing a true statement (changing a number, flipping a comparison) — so the model must actually read the evidence, not pattern-match plausible text. The perturbed_explanation field (shown for refuted items) states exactly what's wrong.

Test set · 2,000 examples across four reasoning types. Below: one Entailed + one Refuted per type.

How to read each example

Claim (amber box) → the sentence to verify  ·  Evidence → the figure/table image(s) it cites  ·  Gold label → the colored badge. Refuted items add a red “Why it's refuted” box; expand “Full metadata” for the original-vs-perturbed pair.

Example 1 — direct Entailed

Direct reasoning. Read a value or trend straight off a single chart/table.

CLAIM (verify against the evidence)

In the seasonal subplot, across the three most prominent peaks, the predicted values (yellow) deviate from the true values (green) by less than 0.1 amplitude units each, indicating high accuracy in capturing peak magnitudes.

Example 2 — direct Refuted

Direct reasoning. Read a value or trend straight off a single chart/table.

CLAIM (verify against the evidence)

The Atlas robot's 3,399 collision pairs exceed H1's 494 collision pairs by over 6-fold.

Why it's refuted. Table 1 shows H1 has 255 collision pairs, not 494. Therefore comparing Atlas’s 3,399 pairs to an incorrect H1 count of 494 is factually wrong.

Example 3 — analytical Entailed

Analytical reasoning. Reason about why — the numbers may read correctly, but the stated cause / interpretation can still be wrong.

CLAIM (verify against the evidence)

CN’s Grade coefficient (−0.982) is more negative than N’s (−0.844), reflecting attenuation bias reversal: incorporating boundary censoring via a log‐σ link reduces variance at 0 and 1, thus amplifying mean‐parameter effects compared to ordinary least squares.

Perturbed (false) statementCN’s Grade coefficient (−0.982) is less negative than N’s (−0.844), reflecting attenuation bias reversal: incorporating boundary censoring via an identity σ link reduces variance at 0.5, thus amplifying mean‐parameter effects compared to ordinary least squares.

Example 4 — analytical Refuted

Analytical reasoning. Reason about why — the numbers may read correctly, but the stated cause / interpretation can still be wrong.

CLAIM (verify against the evidence)

In the imbalanced setting, the LL approach yields delta accuracies below 0.02 on the MNIST task across all four evaluation rounds, indicating near-perfect alignment with the global model due to its local fine-tuning mechanism.

Why it's refuted. This claim is incorrect because Figure 9 shows LL’s delta accuracies for MNIST are approximately 0.08, 0.075, 0.08, and 0.078 across rounds 0–3, well above 0.02, contradicting the stated threshold.

Example 6 — parallel Refuted

Parallel reasoning. Combine evidence from two figures/tables to judge the claim.

CLAIM (verify against the evidence)

On GSM8k, Llama-3.1-70B’s reordering accuracy falls from 93.0% at one shuffle to 89.0% at three shuffles (4-point drop), yet Table 1 shows it retains 97.1% of its original BASE accuracy on average across all operations.

Why it's refuted. This is incorrect because the chart shows Llama-3.1-70B’s accuracy at three reorders is 87.0%, not 89.0%, making the drop 6 points, not 4.0. Moreover, Table 1 reports a 94.2% average retention for Llama-3.1-70B, not 97.1%.

Reasoning typeparallel
Cited section(s)4.2

Perturbed (false) statementOn GSM8k, Llama-3.1-70B’s reordering accuracy falls from 93.0% at one shuffle to 89.0% at three shuffles (4-point drop), yet Table 1 shows it retains 97.1% of its original BASE accuracy on average across all operations.

Example 8 — sequential Refuted

Sequential reasoning. Chained, multi-step reasoning: a result from one item feeds the next.

CLAIM (verify against the evidence)

At input length 4096, DocMamba achieves 3.1 FPS versus LayoutLMv3’s 1.6 FPS—a 1.9× speedup. Given DocMamba₅₁₂ reaches 96.7 % F1 at input length 2560, this implies it can maintain near-97 % accuracy while processing long documents in real time.

Why it's refuted. Figure 5 shows LayoutLMv3’s FPS at input length 4096 is 1.3 FPS, not 1.6 FPS, making the true speedup 2.4× (3.1/1.3) rather than 1.9×. Figure 6 shows DocMamba₅₁₂ attains 98.7 % F1 at length 2560, not 96.7 %, so the accuracy is near-99 %, not near-97 %.

Reasoning typesequential
Cited section(s)5.3

Perturbed (false) statementAt input length 4096, DocMamba achieves 3.1 FPS versus LayoutLMv3’s 1.6 FPS—a 1.9× speedup. Given DocMamba₅₁₂ reaches 96.7 % F1 at input length 2560, this implies it can maintain near-97 % accuracy while processing long documents in real time.
